idiom_name: int64_t id member + sqlite3_last_insert_rowid() / RETURNING id
implementation_notes: C has no mapper, so the identity field is a plain member of the entity struct (int64_t, matching a 64-bit key column) and the key is either read back from the connection - SQLite: sqlite3_last_insert_rowid() after the INSERT, a connection-level value rather than a row-level one - or returned by the statement itself with a RETURNING clause through libpq. The classic key-generator object is replaced by the schema (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY / bigserial) plus that one read; when the key must exist before the INSERT, generate it in the application with libuuid or a ULID/snowflake routine. Hand-written is the norm because there is no dominant C mapper to absorb the field.
pitfalls: sqlite3_last_insert_rowid() belongs to the connection and is unpredictable if another thread inserts on the same connection; it also survives a rollback, so a failed insert still moves the value.
Storing a 64-bit key in int, or printing it with %d, truncates or overflows - use int64_t and PRId64.
0 doubles as 'not persisted' because C has no nullable key type; keep that sentinel inside the mapping layer instead of testing it in domain code.
